analysis.one_liner: Forces Medicare Advantage plans to speed up and publicly report decisions on approving seniors' care.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote in September 2022 with 326 cosponsors, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of seniors in private Medicare Advantage plans face waiting periods before their doctors can provide care or equipment, a process called prior authorization. This bill would require those plans to accept and answer authorization requests electronically, give instant approval for services the plan routinely approves, respond to standard requests within seven days and urgent ones within 24 to 72 hours, and publish annual data on how many requests they deny, how they use artificial intelligence in denials, and how long decisions take. It passed the House by voice vote but never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and people with disabilities enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, whose care is currently subject to plan-by-plan approval delays, plus doctors and providers who navigate the process by fax and payer-specific portals.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Advantage plans must build an electronic prior authorization program and provide real-time decisions for items and services that are routinely approved, ending paper faxes and one-off portals for those requests.

Plans must answer standard prior authorization requests within seven days, and urgent requests within 72 hours or 24 hours when a delay could seriously jeopardize a patient's health, tightening the existing 72-hour standard.

Plans must report annually, on a public Medicare website, the share of requests approved and denied, appeal results, how long decisions took, and how they used artificial intelligence or other decision technology — letting patients, doctors, and regulators see which plans deny the most care.

The bill requires enrollee protections: plans must share their approval criteria with providers and enrollees on request, waive or modify prior authorization for providers with good track records, and review each year which services even need prior authorization.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers bear the compliance cost of building electronic systems and disclosing their denial data, and the bill moves $25 million from Medicare's hospital and outpatient trust funds to fund implementation at CMS.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not limit which items and services Medicare Advantage plans may subject to prior authorization in the first place — plans keep full discretion to require approval for any covered item other than drugs, so care can still be denied after the faster process runs.

The main benefits are delayed: real-time electronic decisions are not required until the third plan year after enactment, and public reporting until the fourth, so patients would have waited years for relief even if it had passed.

Plans face new administrative and reporting burdens, and the bill spends $25 million drawn from the Medicare Hospital Insurance and Supplementary Medical Insurance trust funds to pay for implementation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for patients — faster answers, fewer fax-based delays, and public data on which plans deny the most care — are large and direct, while the costs are mostly administrative burdens on insurers and a modest trust-fund transfer for implementation. The honest limitation is that the bill streamlines and publicizes prior authorization but does not restrain insurers' underlying authority to require it, so it is a transparency fix rather than a coverage fix.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill by voice vote on September 14, 2022, but the Senate never brought it to a vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in May 2021 and drew 326 cosponsors, including 191 Democrats and 135 Republicans, an unusually broad bipartisan base.

After a motion to place it on the Consensus Calendar — a House device for advancing widely supported bills without committee gatekeeping — a Ways and Means subcommittee amended and forwarded it, and the full House passed it by voice vote on September 14, 2022, with no recorded opposition.
The Senate received the bill on September 15, 2022, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without a Senate vote despite passing the House and, under the next Congress, would have had to start over.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers are better off because the bill died: they keep their prior authorization discretion with no requirement to report denial rates, turnaround times, or their use of AI in coverage decisions, and seniors facing care delays gained nothing.

for.name: Suzan DelBene
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and filed the motion that placed it on the Consensus Calendar, clearing the way for House passage.

for.name: 135 of 213 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority support from both parties.

for.name: Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health
for.what_they_did: Held a markup, amended the bill, and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote on the day of House passage.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote in the final months of the 117th Congress; it sat without action after being received on September 15, 2022.

against.name: Medicare Advantage insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Pressed Congress to rely on voluntary industry standards for prior authorization rather than the statutory mandates this bill would impose.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily bipartisan: 326 of 435 House members cosponsored, split 191 Democrats and 135 Republicans, and the House passed it by voice vote with no recorded opposition; the obstacle was Senate inaction, not a party fight.

industries.note: The bill imposes real costs on these insurers — mandatory electronic systems, tight response deadlines, and public disclosure of denial rates, appeal overturns, and AI use — while leaving their core authority to require prior authorization untouched. Their interest in deciding which care gets approved runs against patients waiting for that care, which is why transparency requirements bite hardest on the plans that deny the most.

Providers would send authorization requests electronically and get real-time answers for routine services instead of navigating faxes and plan-specific portals, and they gain access to each plan's approval criteria. Faster approvals mean patients receive care sooner.

The bill creates a federally standardized market for electronic prior authorization systems that all Medicare Advantage plans must adopt, benefiting the vendors that build them. Their gain comes from a service patients also benefit from.
